definition: In this historical context, distinctness refers to the quality of an idea or representation being clearly set off and differentiated, as part of the rational standard of “clearness and distinctness.” Here it is linked with a view of truth that values orderly, intelligible presentation rather than confusion or vagueness.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Art and Art Theories; pinned source text

reasons: The packet only mentions Boileau’s use of “truth” as nearly the same as Descartes’s rational “clearness and distinctness”; it does not explicitly define “distinctness” as a quality of an idea or representation.
The added gloss about orderly, intelligible presentation contrasted with confusion or vagueness is not supported by the packet.
The definition goes beyond the source by turning a brief historical comparison into a general account of the term’s meaning.

The packet does not define “distinctness” as a quality of an idea or representation being “clearly set off and differentiated.” It only mentions that Descartes’s rational standard of “clearness and distinctness” is echoed in Boileau’s use of “truth,” without explaining distinctness in those terms.

The definition links distinctness to a “view of truth” valuing “orderly, intelligible presentation rather than confusion or vagueness,” but the packet does not support that characterization of distinctness or of truth in this way.
While the packet mentions the phrase “clearness and distinctness,” it does not provide the requested sense of the term beyond referencing it as part of Descartes’s rational standard.
